The notch is in the upper lobe.
The notch is anterior.
The diaphragmatic surface is the base.
The cardiac impression is on the mediastinal surface, but the notch is on the anterior border.

explanation.overview: The cardiac notch is an indentation on the anterior border of the left lung, primarily involving the upper lobe.
explanation.highYield: Cardiac notch = anterior border of left upper lobe.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: The cardiac notch creates the area of superficial cardiac dullness on percussion.

questions.question: The vertical (Ewart's) sign of pericardial effusion is dullness to percussion at which area?

options.text: Left infrascapular area (due to compression of left lower lobe)
options.explanation: Ewart's sign is dullness and bronchial breath sounds at the left lung base due to compression by pericardial fluid.
It is on the left side.
It is at the base.
Precordial dullness is in cardiac tamponade but Ewart's sign refers to the lung base.
Ewart's sign is left-sided.

explanation.overview: Ewart's sign is dullness to percussion and bronchial breath sounds at the left lung base due to compression of the left lower lobe by a large pericardial effusion.
explanation.highYield: Ewart's sign = left lung base dullness in pericardial effusion.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Ewart's sign can be a clue to large pericardial effusion.

questions.question: The sympathetic innervation to the heart (cardioaccelerator) arises from which spinal levels?

options.explanation: Cardiac sympathetic fibers originate from T1–T4 and synapse in the cervical sympathetic ganglia.
T5–T9 contribute to the greater splanchnic nerve.
C1–C4 contribute to the phrenic nerve and cervical plexus.
These are lumbar sympathetic outflow.
Sacral parasympathetic outflow.

explanation.overview: Cardiac sympathetic preganglionic fibers arise from T1–T4 and synapse in the superior, middle, and inferior cervical ganglia; postganglionic fibers form the cardiac nerves.
explanation.highYield: Cardiac sympathetic = T1–T4.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Sympathetic stimulation increases heart rate and contractility; stellate ganglion block can be used for refractory angina.

questions.question: The parasympathetic innervation to the heart is provided by which nerve?

options.explanation: The vagus nerve provides parasympathetic fibers to the heart, slowing heart rate and reducing contractility.
The phrenic nerve is motor to the diaphragm.
Sympathetic trunk provides sympathetic innervation.
This is a branch of the vagus supplying the larynx.
Intercostal nerves are somatic.

explanation.overview: Parasympathetic innervation to the heart comes from the vagus nerve (CN X), which slows the heart rate and decreases contractility.
explanation.highYield: Cardiac parasympathetic = vagus nerve.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Vagal maneuvers (carotid sinus massage) can terminate supraventricular tachycardias.

questions.question: The esophageal branches of the left gastric artery ascend through the esophageal hiatus and supply the lower esophagus. These branches are at risk during which procedure?

options.explanation: The branches are within the esophageal hiatus; they can be injured during hiatal surgery.
Fundoplication involves mobilizing the gastric fundus; the left gastric branches may be encountered.

options.text: Both are correct; the branches are at the esophageal hiatus and can be injured in both.
options.explanation: Esophageal branches of the left gastric artery are encountered during esophagectomy and hiatal surgeries.
Thoracentesis does not involve the esophageal hiatus.
Mediastinoscopy does not reach the hiatus.

explanation.overview: The esophageal branches of the left gastric artery ascend through the esophageal hiatus to supply the lower esophagus. They are at risk during esophageal surgeries and fundoplication.
explanation.highYield: Esophageal blood supply from left gastric artery; risk in hiatal surgery.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Ischemia of the esophageal anastomosis after esophagectomy can lead to anastomotic leak.

questions.question: The phrenic nerve provides sensory innervation to all of the following EXCEPT:

options.explanation: The phrenic nerve supplies the central diaphragm.
The phrenic nerve supplies the mediastinal pleura.
The phrenic nerve supplies sensory fibers to the pericardium.
The costal part of the diaphragm receives sensory innervation from lower intercostal nerves, not the phrenic.
The central tendon receives sensory fibers from the phrenic nerve.

explanation.overview: The phrenic nerve provides sensory innervation to the central diaphragm, mediastinal pleura, and pericardium, but the costal diaphragm is innervated by lower intercostal nerves.
explanation.highYield: Costal diaphragm sensory ≠ phrenic nerve.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Diaphragmatic irritation from subphrenic abscess can refer pain to the shoulder (phrenic) or anterior abdominal wall (intercostal).

questions.question: The thoracic duct can be identified during thoracotomy as a thin-walled vessel located between the:

options.explanation: In the thorax, the thoracic duct lies between the esophagus and the azygos vein.
The thoracic duct is on the right, between esophagus and azygos.
The thoracic duct is more posterior.

options.text: Superior vena cava and the aorta
options.explanation: Not the location of the thoracic duct.
Too anterior.

explanation.overview: In the thorax, the thoracic duct lies between the esophagus and the azygos vein, posterior to the esophagus.
explanation.highYield: Thoracic duct location: between esophagus and azygos vein.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: During esophageal surgery, identification and preservation of the thoracic duct is essential to prevent chylothorax.

questions.question: During thoracentesis at the midaxillary line, the needle passes through which layers (in order) to reach the pleural space?

options.text: Skin, superficial fascia, serratus anterior, external intercostal, internal intercostal, innermost intercostal, parietal pleura
options.explanation: The needle passes through these layers at the midaxillary line.
Latissimus dorsi is more posterior.
Pectoralis major is anterior.
Trapezius is posterior.
Rectus abdominis is anterior abdominal wall.

explanation.overview: In the midaxillary line, thoracentesis needle passes through skin, superficial fascia, serratus anterior, external intercostal, internal intercostal, innermost intercostal, and parietal pleura.
explanation.highYield: Thoracentesis layers: skin → serratus anterior → intercostals → pleura.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Knowledge of these layers prevents inadvertent injury to the lung or intercostal vessels.

questions.question: The right coronary artery supplies which of the following in right-dominant circulation?

options.text: Right atrium, right ventricle, SA node (60%), AV node, and inferior wall of left ventricle
options.explanation: In right dominance, RCA supplies the right heart, SA node, AV node, and posterior interventricular septum.

options.text: Only the right atrium and ventricle
options.explanation: It also supplies SA/AV nodes and inferior LV.
Left heart is supplied by left coronary artery.
Anterior wall is LAD territory.
RCA supplies much more.

explanation.overview: In right-dominant circulation, the RCA supplies the right atrium, right ventricle, SA node (60%), AV node, and posterior interventricular septum (inferior LV wall).
explanation.highYield: RCA supplies right heart and inferior wall in right dominance.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Occlusion of RCA can cause inferior MI, often with bradycardia and hypotension.

questions.question: The left coronary artery divides into which two main branches?

options.text: Left anterior descending (LAD) and left circumflex (LCX)
options.explanation: The left main coronary artery bifurcates into the LAD and LCX.
PDA is usually from RCA.
Right coronary is separate.
Acute marginal is from RCA.
Diagonal is a branch of LAD; obtuse marginal is from LCX.

explanation.overview: The left main coronary artery divides into the left anterior descending (LAD) and left circumflex (LCX) arteries.
explanation.highYield: Left coronary artery = LAD + LCX.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Left main stenosis can cause extensive ischemia ('widow maker' if acute occlusion).

questions.question: The azygos vein receives blood from all of the following EXCEPT:

options.explanation: The azygos vein receives right posterior intercostal veins.
The hemiazygos vein drains into the azygos.
The accessory hemiazygos often joins the azygos.
The left superior intercostal vein drains into the left brachiocephalic vein, not the azygos.
Bronchial veins can drain into the azygos system.

explanation.overview: The azygos vein receives the right posterior intercostals, hemiazygos, accessory hemiazygos, and sometimes bronchial veins, but the left superior intercostal vein drains into the left brachiocephalic vein.
explanation.highYield: Left superior intercostal vein → left brachiocephalic, not azygos.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: The azygos system provides an important collateral pathway in SVC obstruction.

questions.question: The pericardial cavity contains serous fluid between which two layers?

options.explanation: The pericardial cavity is the potential space between the parietal and visceral layers of serous pericardium.
The fibrous pericardium is external to the parietal serous layer.
Epicardium is the visceral pericardium; the cavity is outside it.
That is the heart wall layers.
Mediastinal pleura is external to the fibrous pericardium.

explanation.overview: The pericardial cavity is the potential space between the parietal and visceral layers of the serous pericardium, containing 15–50 mL of fluid.
explanation.highYield: Pericardial cavity = between parietal and visceral pericardium.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Pericardial effusion is accumulation of excess fluid in this cavity.

questions.question: The sternoclavicular joint is a saddle-type synovial joint. It is the only bony articulation between the upper limb and the:

options.explanation: The sternoclavicular joint connects the clavicle (upper limb) to the manubrium (axial skeleton).
The rib cage is part of the axial skeleton.
Not directly; the upper limb articulates with the axial skeleton at the sternoclavicular joint.
No.
No.

explanation.overview: The sternoclavicular joint is the only bony articulation between the upper limb and the axial skeleton (manubrium).
explanation.highYield: Sternoclavicular joint = only bony connection of upper limb to axial skeleton.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Dislocation of this joint is rare but can be life-threatening if posterior, compressing mediastinal structures.

questions.question: The xiphoid process is an important landmark because it marks the level of:

options.explanation: The xiphoid is at approximately T9–T10 level.
The liver extends above the xiphoid.
The xiphoid is a landmark for the inferior border of the heart.
The esophageal hiatus is at T10, slightly lower.
The arch is at T4/T5.

explanation.overview: The xiphoid process is approximately at the level of T9–T10 and is used as a landmark for the inferior border of the heart.
explanation.highYield: Xiphoid = T9–T10, inferior heart border.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Chest compressions during CPR should be performed on the lower half of the sternum, above the xiphoid to avoid liver injury.

questions.question: The intercostal nerves (T1–T11) supply the intercostal muscles and skin. The 7th to 11th intercostal nerves continue into the abdominal wall to supply muscles and skin. Which nerve is the subcostal nerve?

options.explanation: The subcostal nerve is the anterior ramus of T12.
T11 is an intercostal nerve.
L1 contributes to the iliohypogastric and ilioinguinal nerves.
T10 is an intercostal nerve.
T8 is an intercostal nerve.

explanation.overview: The subcostal nerve is the anterior ramus of T12, running below the 12th rib.
explanation.highYield: Subcostal nerve = T12.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: The subcostal nerve supplies the skin over the hip and lower abdomen; injury can cause numbness in this area.

questions.question: The first intercostal nerve (T1) contributes to the brachial plexus and has a small intercostal branch. The intercostal branch of T1 supplies which muscles?

options.text: First intercostal muscles (intrinsic hand muscles? Actually T1 is mainly to hand via ulnar nerve, but the intercostal branch is small.)
options.explanation: T1 primarily goes to the brachial plexus for hand muscles, but a small intercostal branch supplies the first intercostal space.
Each intercostal nerve supplies its own space.

options.text: No intercostal muscles; it is entirely to the upper limb
options.explanation: T1 does have a tiny intercostal branch.

options.text: Muscles of the first intercostal space only
options.explanation: The small intercostal branch of T1 supplies the first intercostal muscles.
Not neck muscles.

explanation.overview: The first intercostal nerve (T1) contributes mainly to the brachial plexus, but a small intercostal branch supplies the muscles of the first intercostal space.
explanation.highYield: T1 intercostal branch → first intercostal space.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: T1 dermatome is at the medial aspect of the forearm; loss of sensation here suggests T1 root involvement.

questions.question: The transversus thoracis muscle is located on the inner surface of the anterior chest wall. It originates from the lower sternum and xiphoid and inserts onto the:

options.explanation: Transversus thoracis inserts onto the inner surface of costal cartilages 2–6.
That is more lateral and inferior.
Not a clavicular muscle.
It originates from the sternum, not inserts.
It lies deep to the internal thoracic artery but does not insert on pleura.

explanation.overview: Transversus thoracis originates from the lower sternum and xiphoid, and inserts into the inner surface of costal cartilages 2–6.
explanation.highYield: Transversus thoracis inserts on costal cartilages 2–6.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: This muscle may be used as a landmark during internal thoracic artery harvesting.

questions.question: The internal thoracic artery gives off the superior epigastric artery and musculophrenic artery at which intercostal space?

options.explanation: The internal thoracic artery terminates by dividing into the superior epigastric and musculophrenic arteries at the 6th intercostal space.
Too high; termination is lower.
Slightly lower than actual termination.
Too low.
Termination is at the 6th intercostal space.

explanation.overview: The internal thoracic artery terminates at the 6th intercostal space, dividing into the superior epigastric artery (descending) and musculophrenic artery (lateral).
explanation.highYield: Internal thoracic artery terminates at 6th intercostal space.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: The superior epigastric artery can be used as a collateral pathway in aortic coarctation.

questions.question: The right main bronchus is approximately how long?

options.explanation: The right main bronchus is about 2.5 cm long before giving off the upper lobe bronchus.
The left main bronchus is about 5 cm long.
Too short.
Slightly too long; typical length is 2.5 cm.
Close, but standard is 2.5 cm.

explanation.overview: The right main bronchus is shorter, wider, and more vertical, measuring about 2.5 cm before branching into the upper lobe bronchus.
explanation.highYield: Right main bronchus length = 2.5 cm.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: The short right bronchus is why endotracheal tubes can easily enter the right lung if advanced too far.

questions.question: The left main bronchus is approximately how long?

options.explanation: The left main bronchus is about 5 cm long, longer than the right.
That is the length of the right main bronchus.
Shorter than the actual length.
Close, but standard is 5 cm.
Slightly longer than typical.

explanation.overview: The left main bronchus is longer (about 5 cm) and more horizontal than the right, passing under the aortic arch.
explanation.highYield: Left main bronchus length = 5 cm.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Foreign bodies are less likely to lodge in the left bronchus due to its narrower and more horizontal course.

questions.question: The trachea bifurcates at the carina, which is located at the level of the sternal angle. This corresponds to which thoracic vertebral level?

options.explanation: The carina is at the level of T4/T5 intervertebral disc.
Too high.
Too low.
Slightly higher than the carina.
Slightly lower.

explanation.overview: The tracheal bifurcation (carina) is at the sternal angle, corresponding to T4/T5.
explanation.highYield: Carina = T4/T5.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: The carina is a landmark for bronchoscopy and for determining proper endotracheal tube placement.

questions.question: The bronchopulmonary segments are independent units of the lung with their own bronchus, artery, and vein. How many segments are in the right lung?

options.explanation: The right lung has 10 bronchopulmonary segments: upper lobe (3), middle lobe (2), lower lobe (5).
The left lung has 8–10 segments, but the right has 10.
The right lung has 10.
There are 10 segments in the right lung.
Too few.

explanation.overview: The right lung has 10 bronchopulmonary segments: 3 in the upper lobe, 2 in the middle lobe, and 5 in the lower lobe.
explanation.highYield: Right lung = 10 bronchopulmonary segments.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Knowledge of segments is critical for segmental resection and interpreting imaging.

questions.question: How many bronchopulmonary segments are typically found in the left lung?

options.explanation: The left lung usually has 8–10 segments; the apical and posterior segments of the upper lobe are often fused, giving 8.
The left lung often has fewer due to fusion.
Too few.
Too many.
It can vary; typical is 8 but may be 9 or 10.

explanation.overview: The left lung typically has 8–10 bronchopulmonary segments, often 8 due to fusion of the apicoposterior segment in the upper lobe.
explanation.highYield: Left lung segments = usually 8 (fusion of apical and posterior).
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Surgical planning for left lung resections must account for this anatomical variation.

questions.question: The pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood. At the lung root, the pulmonary artery is located:

options.text: Superior to the bronchus on the left, and anterior to the bronchus on the right
options.explanation: At the right hilum, the pulmonary artery is anterior to the bronchus; on the left, it is superior to the bronchus.

options.text: Posterior to the bronchus on both sides
options.explanation: It is anterior/superior, not posterior.

options.text: Inferior to the bronchus on both sides
options.explanation: The pulmonary veins are inferior.

options.text: Superior to the bronchus on the right
options.explanation: On the right, the artery is anterior, not superior.
Not posterior.

explanation.overview: At the right hilum, the pulmonary artery is anterior to the bronchus; at the left hilum, it is superior to the bronchus (mnemonic: RALS – Right Anterior, Left Superior).
explanation.highYield: Pulmonary artery: right = anterior, left = superior to bronchus.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: This relationship is key for interpreting chest X-ray hilar anatomy.

questions.question: The ligamentum arteriosum connects which two structures?

options.text: Pulmonary trunk to the aortic arch
options.explanation: The ligamentum arteriosum is the fibrous remnant of the ductus arteriosus, connecting the pulmonary trunk to the aortic arch.

options.text: Aorta to the superior vena cava
options.explanation: No such connection.

options.text: Pulmonary veins to the left atrium
options.explanation: The pulmonary veins directly enter the left atrium.

options.text: Right pulmonary artery to the aortic arch
options.explanation: The ligamentum arteriosum connects the pulmonary trunk, not the right pulmonary artery.

options.text: Left subclavian artery to the left common carotid
options.explanation: They are separate branches of the aortic arch.

explanation.overview: The ligamentum arteriosum is the remnant of the ductus arteriosus, connecting the left pulmonary artery (or pulmonary trunk) to the inferior aspect of the aortic arch.
explanation.highYield: Ligamentum arteriosum = pulmonary trunk to aortic arch.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: A patent ductus arteriosus is a congenital heart defect where this connection remains open, causing a continuous murmur.
